questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in future perfect tense form.

I hope you wash all the clothes before you come into the house again.

options.text: I hope you will have washed all the clothes before you come into the house again.
I hope you shall wash all the clothes before you come into the house again.
I hope you will be washing all the clothes before you come into the house again.
I hope you will have wash all the clothes before you come into the house again.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The future perfect tense is used to describe an action that will be completed before a specific time in the future.
 
• The structure of the future perfect tense is: **will/shall + have + past participle**.
 
• In the given sentence, the action of washing all the clothes is expected to be completed before the action of coming into the house again.
 
• Option 1, "I hope you will have washed all the clothes before you come into the house again," correctly uses the future perfect tense ("will have washed") for the first action.

Therefore, the correct answer is **1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"I hope you **will have washed** all the clothes before you come into the house again."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **2) I hope you shall wash all the clothes before you come into the house again.** – This option uses the simple future tense ("shall wash"), not the future perfect. While "shall" can be used for the future, "will" is more common in modern English for most subjects.
 
• **3) I hope you will be washing all the clothes before you come into the house again.** – This option uses the future continuous tense ("will be washing"), which describes an ongoing action in the future, not a completed one before another future action.
 
• **4) I hope you will have wash all the clothes before you come into the house again.** – This option incorrectly uses the base form of the verb "wash" after "will have." The past participle ("washed") is required for the future perfect tense.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required.'

We made sure our new house __were closer__ to a good primary school when moving home last summer.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **was close**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Was** should be used here instead of **were**.
 
• **Was** is the** first and third-person singular past tense **of the verb **to be**, while **were** is the **second-person singular past and plural past** of the verb **to be**.
 
• **Out new house** is **singular** and therefore, the use of **was** is more appropriate here. 
 
• Thus, the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence is** option 1**.

questions.question: From the given options, identify the sentence which is in the positive degree.

options.text: I have a greater idea in this regard.
His brother is an intelligent boy.
She is the most beautiful girl of the class.
They are playing hockey with longer sticks.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **positive degree** is used to describe a quality without making any comparison, such as simply stating a fact or characteristic.
 
• In the sentence "**His brother is an intelligent boy**," the adjective "intelligent" is in the **positive degree** as it simply describes his brother without comparing him to anyone else.
 
• The other options use comparative or superlative degrees: 
 
 
• **Option 1:** "Greater" is a **comparative degree**, indicating a comparison of two things.
 
• **Option 3:** "Most beautiful" is a **superlative degree**, indicating the highest degree of beauty among a group.
 
• **Option 4:** "Longer" is a **comparative degree**, comparing the sticks to others.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"His brother is an intelligent boy."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **positive degree** simply describes a quality without comparing it to others (e.g., smart, beautiful, tall).
 
• The **comparative degree** is used to compare two things (e.g., smarter, more beautiful, taller).
 
• The **superlative degree** is used to compare more than two things and shows the highest or lowest degree of a quality (e.g., smartest, most beautiful, tallest).

questions.question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

He gritted his teeth and tried to act as though he (either noticed nor cared).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**neither noticed nor cared.**"

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The original sentence contains an error in parallelism, as it uses "either" without also using "or" to create a balanced structure.
 
• The correct phrase should be "neither...nor," which is a common idiomatic expression in English.
 
• We use neither as a conjunction with nor. It connects two or more negative alternatives.
 
• In the given sentence, it is mentioned that the subject acted as if did not care or noticed.
 
• Thus, the correct sentence will be:
 
 
• He gritted his teeth and tried to act as though he neither noticed nor cared.
 
 

Hence, **the correct answer is option 1**

questions.question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

I rode my bike to __worked those__ morning
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'Option 4'** i.e.** "work this."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence* "I rode my bike to 'worked those' morning"* is grammatically incorrect.
 
• The correct phrase should be **"work this,".**
 
• **"work this" -** This is the correct answer. The noun "work" denotes the place of employment, and "this" correctly refers to the current morning.

Therefore, the **correct sentence** is: *"I rode my bike to work this morning".*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Here's the explanation:
 
 
• **"worked this" **- This option is incorrect because "worked" is a verb in the past tense. We need a noun, which is "work," to denote the place where one is employed. Also, "this" is correct as it refers to the current day.
 
• **"work these"** - This option is incorrect. The word "these" is a plural demonstrative pronoun and doesn't fit in this context. We're referring to a single, specific morning (the one today), so we should use "this."

questions.question: Select the grammatically correct sentence.

options.text: The traffic on a highway was heavy during an evening.
The traffic on the highway was heavy during the evening.
The traffic on the highway was heavy during an evening.
A traffic on the highway was heavy during an evening.

questions.solution:
**The correct answer is option 2.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

**Let's analyze each sentence to determine the grammatically correct option:**

__
 
• **1) The traffic on a highway was heavy during an evening.**

 
 
• While "a highway" is grammatically correct, "an evening" is less natural. We usually refer to a specific part of the day with "the" when it's implied or understood.
 
 
 
• **2) The traffic on the highway was heavy during the evening.**
 
 
• "The traffic" is appropriate as traffic is generally considered a singular mass noun in this context. "The highway" implies a specific highway, which is natural. "During the evening" is the standard and grammatically correct way to refer to that part of the day.
 
• This sentence is grammatically and contextually correct__.
 
 
 
• **3) The traffic on the highway was heavy during an evening.**
 
 
• Similar to option 1, "an evening" is less natural than "the evening."
 
 
 
• **4) A traffic on the highway was heavy during an evening.**
 
 
• "Traffic" is generally an uncountable noun, so it doesn't typically take the indefinite article "a." We say "heavy traffic," not "a traffic." Also, "an evening" is less natural.
 
 

**Based on the analysis, option 2 uses the articles "the" appropriately for both "traffic," "highway," and "evening" in this context.**

**Therefore, the grammatically correct sentence is:**

**The traffic on the highway was heavy during the evening.**
